---
title: "Socioeconomic variables"
subtitle: "Education, income and employment following the SEPLINE approach"
date: last-modified
---

You now know the pattern:
`read_register/open_dataset → filter → collect → left_join`. That is exactly
what you use here. Two things are **new** in this phase:

1. **"Fetch for the year before index date":** SES registers are annual
   snapshots. You cannot just filter on `pnr`; you must also match on *which
   year* is relevant per person (`year(index_date) - 1`). This is done by
   calculating the baseline year per person and using it as a join key.
2. **FAIK via `familie_id`:** Income is linked to the *household*, not the
   person directly. You need BEF as a bridge: fetch `familie_id` from BEF for
   the baseline year, then join to FAIK on `familie_id`.

The rest is categorisation per SEPLINE guidelines.

Socioeconomic position (SEP) is measured in register-based studies via three
dimensions: education (UDDA), income (FAIK) and employment (AKM). This page
shows how to extract and categorise them following the **SEPLINE** guideline.

**SEPLINE article:** Hjorth et al. *Clinical Epidemiology* 2025 -
[doi:10.2147/CLEP.S520772](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772). See the
article for full justification, recommended reference groups and
categorisations.

::: {.callout-important title="Structural guidance, not verified code"}
The categorisations below are **not validated**. They show how to code the
variables, not an approved implementation, so review them against your own
analysis plan before you use them. Have working code, or input on the
categorisations? [Get in touch](contribute.qmd).
:::

The examples read registers by name with `read_register()`, which assumes
[fastreg is pointed at your registers](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#fastreg-paths).
Without fastreg, use `open_dataset("path/to/akm/")` instead. Column names differ
between deliveries, so check yours with `names(your_data)`.


::: {.callout-warning}
**Fetch the variable for the year BEFORE index by default - but SEPLINE does
not use one timing rule for all three dimensions.** All three registers are
**annual**: each person has one value per calendar year. If you take the value
from the *index year* itself, you risk measuring status that falls **after**
your exposure. Example: index = surgery date 15 June 2015. The 2015 value may
reflect status after the surgery and be affected by the exposure itself (e.g.
job loss after illness) - that gives reverse causation, whereas you want a
**baseline** value from before the exposure.

`year(index_date) - 1` is a safe default, and this page uses it throughout for
consistency. But SEPLINE's own tables set the timing per dimension, not once
for all three:

- **Income** (Table 8): strictly the **three years preceding** the index
  year, never the index year itself - no ambiguity here, see the income
  section below.
- **Employment** (Table 5): "the latest available status at index date," in
  practice the year before index for AKM's annual snapshot. SEPLINE's own
  caveat: go earlier still if your specific outcome carries a strong
  reverse-causation risk, or use DREAM instead of AKM if you need
  closer-to-index granularity (DREAM updates weekly, not annually).
- **Education** (Table 2): "the latest available educational level at index
  date" - not the year before. A completed degree cannot be undone by
  illness, so education does not carry the same reverse-causation risk as
  employment or income. See the [education section's own
  callout](#education) for how to follow this looser rule instead of the
  page's default.

So `year(index_date) - 1` is this page's uniform *default*, not SEPLINE's
uniform *rule* - know the difference before you defend the choice in a methods
section.
:::

## The three dimensions

  | Dimension      | Register | Variable                                                      |
  | -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | **Education**  | UDDA     | `hfaudd` - highest completed education (DISCED-15 code)      |
  | **Income**     | FAIK     | `famaekvivadisp_13` - household-equivalised disposable income |
  | **Employment** | AKM      | `socio13` - labour market classification                      |

SEPLINE specifies both **how** these variables are categorised and **when** in
the follow-up they are measured.

## Before you extract anything: give the cohort a stable row id

::: {.callout-note}
**This page joins on `row_id`, not `pnr`, throughout.** If your cohort has
exactly one row per person, that makes no difference to you - skip ahead. If
it does not (e.g. a comparison group matched **with replacement**, see
[comparison cohort's note on
it](comparison-cohort.qmd#step-4---assemble-validate-and-save)), `row_id` is
what keeps a repeated `pnr`'s different `index_date`s from getting mixed up
in the joins below - with no error and no `NA` to flag it if it went wrong.
:::

```r
library(dplyr) # mutate, left_join, group_by, summarise, bind_rows
library(lubridate) # year() to extract year from a date

cohort <- cohort %>%
  mutate(
    row_id = row_number(), # one id per cohort row - stays unique even if pnr repeats
    year_baseline = lubridate::year(index_date) - 1 # baseline year, computed once and reused below
  )
```

Every join from here on uses `row_id` (to attach a finished variable back onto
`cohort`) or `pnr` + `year_baseline` together (to pull a value out of a
register) - never `pnr` by itself.

::: {.callout-important}
**A `collect()`ed register extract only contains rows that matched your
filter.** Someone with zero qualifying records - no UDDA row before their
baseline year, no AKM row for their exact baseline year, no household match in
BEF - is simply **absent** from that table, not present with an `NA`. Left-join
such a table onto your cohort and those people get `NA` for the derived
variable.

That matters more than it looks. Most R modelling functions, including
`survival::coxph()`, drop any row with an `NA` covariate by default
(`na.action = na.omit`) - **silently, with no warning**. A person with unknown
education does not become an "Unknown" category in your model, they vanish
from the analysis entirely, and your model's N no longer matches your
cohort's N.

The fix used throughout this page: **join onto the full cohort (via `row_id`)
before you categorise, not after.** Then `case_when(... TRUE ~ "Unknown")`
catches the `NA` and turns it into an explicit category, the same way it
already catches any other unmatched code. The `stopifnot(nrow(...) ==
nrow(cohort))` checks in the code below exist to confirm this: as long as row
counts hold at every step, nobody has been silently dropped. Before you trust
a downstream model, also check its N against your cohort's N directly -
this exact pattern (register extract → collect → categorise → model) is not
specific to SES variables, so the same check is worth applying anywhere else
in your pipeline that joins a register onto a cohort and feeds the result
into a regression.
:::

## Employment - AKM (`socio13`)

`socio13` is DST's socioeconomic classification. The full code list, with what
each value means, is in DST's classification documentation:
[SOCIO →](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/nomenklaturer/socio).

::: {.callout-note}
**DST's words are narrower than the everyday ones.** "Beskæftiget" is a
statistical definition with thresholds attached, not simply "has a job", and the
same goes for "husstand" and "disponibel indkomst" further down this page. If
you are about to write in a methods section what a category means, look the word
up first: [Hvad betyder
→](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/hvadbetyder). Getting this
wrong does not produce an error, it produces a sentence in your paper that does
not match your data.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Two codes are easy to get wrong.** `410` is **Andre**, a category of its own,
not unemployed: the unemployed are `210`. And `420` is **children under 15**, a
real category rather than a missing value, so seeing it in an adult cohort means
the index date is wrong, not that the data is incomplete.

**SEPLINE's own table does not agree with itself on `410`.** Its Table 6
lists code `410` in two different rows at once: under "B1: Unemployed (210,
410)" *and* under "Missing/other." We checked this directly against the
published PDF at 400 DPI, not a scraped summary - it really is listed twice,
not a misread on our part. This page keeps `410` as its own "Other" category,
matching DST's own "Andre" label, rather than silently picking one of
SEPLINE's two contradictory placements. Folding `410` into "Unemployed"
instead, to match Table 6's B1 row, is also defensible - just document which
reading you used and why, since the source itself does not resolve it.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**AKM has a documented gap in 2014.** SEPLINE's Table 4 (Data Sources for
Labor Market Affiliation) states, without further detail: *"Data gap in
2014."* Nothing elsewhere in the article says what the gap actually is - a
missing year entirely, partial coverage, or specific codes affected - so
check your own extract before trusting any 2014 `socio13` value:

```r
akm %>% filter(year == 2014) %>% count(socio13) %>% collect()
```

Compare the total row count and code distribution against a neighbouring
year. If your cohort has baseline years in 2014, resolve this before you
trust that year's employment status.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Two things about `year` before you join on it.** It is not a DST variable - it
comes from the parquet partitioning, so confirm the name in your own files
([Phase 4](file-formats.qmd#year-column)). And do not assign to it: `mutate(year
= ...)` overwrites the partition column rather than adding one, which silently
breaks every join in this chapter, since they all join on person plus year. Give
a derived year its own name, e.g. `index_year`.
:::


```r
library(fastreg) # read_register() - reads registers by name
library(arrow) # open_dataset() - fallback without fastreg

# 1. Open AKM via fastreg (read_register gets the path from your project config)
akm <- read_register("akm") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) # standardise column names
# Without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/akm/") %>% rename_with(tolower)

# 2. Fetch employment status for every baseline year the cohort needs.
# unique() here is only an efficiency filter: cohort$year_baseline has one
# value PER ROW (with repeats - many people share a baseline year), and
# unique() collapses that to the distinct set of years so the query below
# does not re-read a year twice. It does NOT pair a year back to a person -
# that pairing happens in step 3, via the join, using pnr + year_baseline
# together.
index_year <- unique(cohort$year_baseline)

# copy = TRUE: akm is a remote/database connection (fastreg may route through
# DuckDB), tibble(pnr = ...) is a local R object. dplyr will not silently join
# across two different sources - copy = TRUE is your explicit permission to
# copy the small local pnr list into the database so the join can run there.
# Without it the join errors outright (it does not affect correctness, only
# whether the code runs at all) - needed on every semi_join in this pattern,
# not just this one, e.g. also for LPR extracts.
akm_data <- akm %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # only the cohort's pnr's
  filter(year %in% !!index_year) %>% # only years the cohort actually needs
  select(pnr, year, socio13) %>% # only the columns we use
  collect() # fetch into R

# 3. Attach to cohort - one row per cohort row, matched to THAT row's own
# baseline year (year_baseline already exists on cohort, see "Before you
# extract anything" above)
cohort_akm <- cohort %>%
  left_join(akm_data, by = c("pnr", "year_baseline" = "year")) # pnr + year together, not pnr alone

# Sanity check: a correct join never changes the row count
stopifnot(nrow(cohort_akm) == nrow(cohort))

# 4. Categorise per SEPLINE
cohort_akm <- cohort_akm %>%
  mutate(
    occupation_cat = case_when(
      socio13 %in%
        c(
          110,
          111,
          112,
          113,
          114,
          120,
          131,
          132,
          133,
          134,
          135,
          139
        ) ~ "Employed",
      socio13 == 310 ~ "Student", # under uddannelse
      socio13 == 210 ~ "Unemployed", # arbejdsløse mindst halvdelen af året
      # 220 sygedagpenge/orlov, 321 førtidspension, 330 kontanthjælp
      socio13 %in% c(220, 321, 330) ~ "Outside labour market",
      socio13 %in% c(322, 323) ~ "Retired", # folkepension, efterløn
      socio13 == 410 ~ "Other", # "Andre" - a category of its own, not unemployed
      socio13 == 420 ~ "Child under 15", # should not occur in an adult cohort
      TRUE ~ "Unknown" # missing
    )
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Check your AKM before you trust this join"}
The recipe above assumes **one row per `pnr` per year** in `akm_data` - that
is why the join on `pnr` + `year_baseline` does not need a dedup step.
SEPLINE's own description of `socio13` backs this up: "employed individuals
are registered based on their main occupation during a given year, based on
the activity that generated the largest amount of income" (Hjorth et al.
2025, [doi:10.2147/CLEP.S520772](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772), Table
6, Labor Market Affiliation). DST resolves multiple jobs to one code *before*
the register is delivered, so a standard AKM delivery should not have
duplicates.

SEPLINE later published a
[corrigendum](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S612503) (Hjorth et al. 2026) to
that same Table 6: it adds DREAM codes for people awaiting a flex job (740,
743--748) that the original table missed, and merges the old Senior Pension
code into C3 Disability Pension, noting that Statistics Denmark confirmed both
schemes fall under `socio13` code `321`. It does **not** touch the
main-occupation rule quoted above, and says nothing about handling multiple
jobs or codes within a year - so do not lean on the corrigendum for that
question, it fixes a different part of the table.

**Whether your delivery matches this depends on your data, so check rather
than assume:**

```r
akm_data %>%
  count(pnr, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1)
```

**If this is empty:** `socio13` is already the dominant occupation, nothing
further needed.

**If it is not empty:** first drop exact duplicates - same `pnr`, `year` and
`socio13` repeated:

```r
akm_data <- akm_data %>%
  distinct(pnr, year, socio13) # one row per person per year
```

Re-run the count above. Rows that still differ in `socio13` for the same
person-year are not something SEPLINE or DST resolves for you: the
corrigendum patches a different part of Table 6, not this. If you still need
one row per person-year, pick a **tie-break priority order** and document it,
rather than choosing silently - e.g. ranked by attachment to the labour
market, using the `occupation_cat` grouping from step 4 above (not raw
`socio13`, which is a code list, not a scale):

`Employed > Student > Unemployed > Outside labour market > Retired > Other > Unknown`

This ordering is **our own convention, not SEPLINE's** - review it against
your own analysis plan before using it.
:::

## Education - UDDA (`hfaudd`) {#education}

`hfaudd` is short for **h**øjest **f**uldførte **AUDD** - the highest completed
education, coded with an **AUDD** code. It is a four-digit DISCED-15 code for
the **specific education** a person completed: `4112` is "electrician". It is an
identifier, not a scale, so the level (short / medium / long) has to be **looked
up**, not read off the digits. UDDA itself does not carry the level.

The `AUDD` in the name matters when you go looking for a lookup table: DISCED-15
codes come in two flavours, **AUDD** for a *completed* education and **UDD** for
one that is ongoing or was interrupted. DST documents them as two separate
classifications, [DISCED-15 AUDD](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/nomenklaturer/disced15-audd) and [DISCED-15
UDD](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/nomenklaturer/disced15-udd). `hfaudd` is completed, so it is an `audd` lookup you want.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not derive the level from `substr(hfaudd, 1, 2)`.** The level codes (10, 15,
20, 30, 40, 70, 90) look just like the first two digits of an education code, so
it is the obvious thing to try - and it is wrong roughly 4 times in 10, silently.
You need the lookup. Why it fails is set out in [Overview of
registers](register-reference.qmd#udda---education-register).
:::

```r
# 1. Open UDDA via fastreg (read_register gets the path from your project config)
udda <- read_register("udda") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) # standardise column names
# Without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/udda/") %>% rename_with(tolower)

# 2. Fetch every education record up to the latest baseline year anyone in the
# cohort needs (broader than AKM/FAIK's exact-year filter on purpose - step 3
# below needs each row's history, not just its one exact baseline year).
udda_data <- udda %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # only the cohort's pnr's, copy = TRUE: see AKM step 2
  filter(year <= max(cohort$year_baseline)) %>% # every year any row could fall back to
  select(pnr, year, hfaudd) %>% # only the columns we use
  collect() # fetch into R

stopifnot(nrow(udda_data) > 0)

# 3. For each cohort row, keep its OWN most recent record at or before ITS
# baseline year - not a global "newest year fetched" (the earlier version of
# this page did that with group_by(pnr) %>% slice(1), which silently hands a
# later row's education to an earlier row once the same pnr repeats with two
# different baseline years - see "Before you extract anything" above). This
# also means a gap in the exact baseline year no longer becomes a missing
# value: the most recent earlier record carries forward, since a completed
# education does not regress. left_join (not inner_join) keeps rows for
# people with zero UDDA records too, as NA - see the NA-vs-Unknown callout
# above for why that matters.
cohort_udda <- cohort %>%
  select(row_id, pnr, year_baseline) %>%
  left_join(udda_data, by = "pnr", relationship = "many-to-many") %>% # every row x every record for that pnr, on purpose
  filter(is.na(year) | year <= year_baseline) %>% # only records at or before this row's own baseline
  group_by(row_id) %>%
  slice_max(year, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% # this row's own most recent record
  ungroup()

stopifnot(nrow(cohort_udda) == nrow(cohort))

# 4. Look the level up - one row per education code, joined on hfaudd
library(heaven) # edu_code: 4,621 DISCED-15 codes with their level
data(edu_code)

cohort_udda <- cohort_udda %>%
  mutate(hfaudd = as.character(hfaudd)) %>% # match the type in edu_code
  left_join(
    edu_code %>%
      as_tibble() %>% # edu_code is a data.table
      mutate(hfaudd = as.character(hfaudd)) %>%
      select(hfaudd, level_code = number), # number = the two-digit level
    by = "hfaudd"
  )

# 5. Group the level into the SEPLINE categories
cohort_udda <- cohort_udda %>%
  mutate(
    level_code = as.numeric(level_code),
    education_cat = case_when(
      level_code %in% c(5, 10, 15) ~ "Short", # pre-school, primary, preparatory
      level_code %in% c(20, 25, 29, 30, 35, 39) ~ "Medium", # upper secondary and vocational
      level_code >= 40 & level_code < 90 ~ "Long", # short cycle higher and above
      TRUE ~ "Unknown" # 90 "not stated", no UDDA record at all, or no match in edu_code
    )
  )

# ALWAYS check how many did not match - a high number means a type mismatch
# on hfaudd, or codes that are not in the lookup.
cohort_udda %>%
  summarise(unmatched = sum(is.na(level_code)), total = n())
```

::: {.callout-note}
**SEPLINE actually allows a looser cutoff than this code uses.** Table 2 of
the article times education at "the latest available educational level at
index date" - not the year before, unlike employment and income. The
reasoning is specific to education: a completed degree cannot be undone by
your exposure, so there is no reverse-causation risk to guard against by
stepping back a year. This code still uses `year_baseline` (before index) to
stay consistent with the rest of the page and err conservative. If you want
to follow SEPLINE's literal rule, replace `year_baseline` with
`lubridate::year(index_date)` in step 3's filter (and fetch one more year in
step 2) to allow records from the index year itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
**Getting `heaven` outside DST.** On DST it is already installed, which matters
because the server has no internet - you could not install it there yourself.
Elsewhere it is not on CRAN, so `install.packages("heaven")` will not find it,
but it installs from GitHub in one line:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("tagteam/heaven")
```

**If you would rather not add the dependency, DST has the same lookup on the
server.** The level files live in
`SAS_datasaet/Uddannelser/` and are named by the levels they map between: an
**L1 → L5** file turns the four-digit `hfaudd` into the Hovedgruppe (`10
Grundskole`, `20 Gymnasiale`, `30 Erhvervsfaglige`, ... `80 Ph.d.`). [Format
tables](formatting-tables.qmd#education-level) has the naming systematics, the
code, and the three things to check first.

Whichever source you use, the shape of the solution is the same: a table of
education codes joined to your data on `hfaudd`. What you must not do is skip
the lookup.

::: {.callout-important}
**Use one lookup for the whole study, and write down which one.** DST's folder
holds several versions of the classification side by side (`2008`, `2011`,
`2015`, possibly newer). You do not need one per study year: DST updates the
newest version with older codes as well, so the latest file covers your whole
period. Take the newest.

The two routes will not necessarily give you the *same set of categories*
though. `heaven::edu_code` follows DISCED-15 and splits education into 15
groups; DST's level-5 Hovedgruppe is a nine-way split. Neither is wrong - they
are different levels of detail. Compare them on your own data before you commit,
and report which one you used.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
**The grouping in step 5 is our reading of SEPLINE, not a validated
implementation.** `edu_code` gives you the level reliably; how those levels are
collapsed into "short / medium / long" is a study-design choice. Check the
[SEPLINE article](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S520772) for the categorisation
your analysis should use, and note that `edu_code` also carries a ready-made
5-level grouping (`code5txt`) and ISCED codes (`isced_code`) if either fits
better.
:::

## Income - FAIK via BEF (`famaekvivadisp_13`) {#faik-income}

Income is linked to the household, not the person. You need `familie_id` from
BEF as a bridge. SEPLINE's actual rule (Table 8, "Data Management of Income
and Wealth"): average the **three calendar years preceding the year of
index** (not the index year itself, to avoid reverse causation), then classify
into quintiles **stratified by sex × 5-year age group × calendar year**,
computed against the **general population** - not your own cohort's
distribution. The suggested output is 3 categories, not 5 (Table 9): quintile
1 = Low, quintiles 2-4 = Medium, quintile 5 = High.

`famaekvivadisp_13` has a sister column, `famaekvivadisp`, with no suffix. The
`_13` one is not simply the newer of the two: DST gives the old column the years
1990-2012 and the `_13` column 1987-2024, so the newer definition was applied
backwards as well as forwards. Use `_13` for the whole period. Splicing the two
at 2013 mixes two definitions inside one series.

```r
# 1. Open BEF + FAIK via fastreg (read_register gets the path from your project config)
bef <- read_register("bef") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)
faik <- read_register("faik") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) # check whether FAIK is one row per family in YOUR data - see the callout below
# Without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/bef/") %>% rename_with(tolower)  (same for faik)

# 2. Fetch familie_id from BEF for every baseline year the cohort needs (see AKM step 2 for what unique() does)
bef_family <- bef %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # only the cohort's pnr's, copy = TRUE: see AKM step 2
  filter(year %in% !!index_year) %>% # only years the cohort actually needs
  select(pnr, year, familie_id) %>% # familie_id is the bridge to FAIK
  collect() # fetch into R

# 3. Fetch income from FAIK for the same years
faik_data <- faik %>%
  filter(year %in% !!index_year) %>% # only years the cohort actually needs
  select(familie_id, year, famaekvivadisp_13) %>% # only the columns we use
  collect() # fetch into R

# 4. Attach to cohort - one row per cohort row, matched to THAT row's own baseline year
cohort_income <- cohort %>%
  left_join(bef_family, by = c("pnr", "year_baseline" = "year")) %>% # this row's own household, for its own baseline year
  left_join(faik_data, by = c("familie_id", "year_baseline" = "year")) # then that household's income, same year

stopifnot(nrow(cohort_income) == nrow(cohort))
```

This single-year version is here to show the join shape. SEPLINE's actual
income measure is the 3-year mean below - `cohort_income` is not what carries
through to the final assembly.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Check your FAIK before you trust this join"}
The recipe above assumes FAIK holds **one row per family per year** - that is
why the bridge goes through `familie_id`. On DARTER that stopped being true from
**2022 onward**: FAIK now also carries `pnr`, and each family's row is repeated
once per family member. **Whether this applies to your project depends on your
data delivery, so check rather than assume either way.**

```r
names(faik) # is pnr among the columns?

# More than one row per family and year means the duplication applies to you
faik %>%
  count(familie_id, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  count() %>%
  collect()
```

**What it does to the code above.** The join on `familie_id` + `year` returns one
row per family *member* instead of one per person, so your dataset grows without
any error. And the 3-year average further down is then computed over a set
weighted by household size: a five-person family counts five times as much as a
single person in the same year. The numbers stay plausible throughout, which is
what makes it dangerous.

**If it applies to you, one line before the join fixes it.** Collapse the
duplicates back to one row per family-year, and the rest of the recipe works
unchanged for every year:

```r
faik <- faik %>%
  distinct(familie_id, year, famaekvivadisp_13) # one row per household per year
```

If your FAIK carries `pnr` for **all** years, you can join income to `pnr`
directly and skip the BEF bridge entirely.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**A ready-made alternative:
[`heaven::averageIncome()`](packages-overview.qmd#heaven---danish-register-data-toolkit)**
does the multi-year average in one call, uses only the years strictly before the
index year, and keeps one row per person-year - so repeated rows for the same
person and year collapse on their own. That happens to cover the FAIK
duplication above, though the function was written for a different reason
(quarterly duplicates), so do not treat it as a guarantee.

It does **not** replace the BEF bridge: the income table you hand it must
already be linked to `pnr`. `heaven` is pre-installed on DST and installs from
GitHub elsewhere (`pak::pak("tagteam/heaven")`), so the choice is about whether
you want the dependency - the code below is the version with no packages beyond
the ones you already use.
:::

<details>
<summary>3-year average and quintiles (SEPLINE recommendation)</summary>

This is a worked implementation of Table 8's rule, not a simplified stand-in -
see the callouts below for its cost and the choices it still leaves to you.

::: {.callout-warning}
**This works with BEF and FAIK for the whole Danish population, not just
your cohort.** Steps 5-6 below deliberately drop the `pnr` filter, because
SEPLINE stratifies income quintiles against the **general population**
(Table 8, "Standardization"), not against your own cohort's distribution -
`ntile(mean_income, 5)` on the cohort alone answers a different question (how
your participants rank against *each other*, not against the population).

**RAM: the filtering and averaging stay inside the database, not in R.**
Steps 5-6 hold off on `collect()` until after `group_by()`/`summarise(mean(
...))` has already run, so what actually reaches R is one row per
(person, sex, age-group) - not the raw population x 3-years join, which would
be tens of millions of rows. This was checked against a local DuckDB (`year()`,
`floor()` and `mean()` all translate to SQL and run there), not against a real
DST session - if your fastreg setup routes through something else, watch for
whether `collect()` in step 6 is doing more work than expected, and consider
caching the resulting `population_income`/`cutpoints` and reusing them across
runs rather than recomputing every time regardless.

**Using a different reference population is a legitimate choice, but document
it as a deviation.** If you use a comparator arm from your own study instead
of the full population (e.g. because eligibility criteria like "no prior
surgery" or "≥5 years residency" make it a more relevant comparison for your
specific outcome), say so explicitly - the mechanics below are identical, but
the result is no longer SEPLINE's "general population" cutpoints.
:::

```r
library(dplyr) # filter, select, left_join, group_by, summarise, mutate, bind_rows
library(lubridate) # year() to extract year from a date

# 1. The three calendar years SEPLINE asks for: the year before index, and
# the two years before that (Table 8, "Time of measurement") - never the
# index year itself, to avoid reverse causation
income_years <- unique(c(cohort$year_baseline, cohort$year_baseline - 1, cohort$year_baseline - 2))

# 2. Each cohort row needs its OWN 3-year window - not one window shared by
# the whole cohort (see "Before you extract anything" above: the same pnr can
# carry more than one baseline year). Build one row per (cohort row x year
# needed) first, so the years stay tied to the row they belong to:
cohort_income_years <- bind_rows(
  cohort %>% transmute(row_id, pnr, year = year_baseline), # baseline year
  cohort %>% transmute(row_id, pnr, year = year_baseline - 1), # 1 year before
  cohort %>% transmute(row_id, pnr, year = year_baseline - 2) # 2 years before
)

bef_3yr <- bef %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort$pnr), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # only the cohort's pnr's, copy = TRUE: see AKM step 2
  filter(year %in% !!income_years) %>% # only years the cohort actually needs
  select(pnr, year, familie_id, koen, foed_dag) %>% # koen + foed_dag needed for the sex x age strata in step 8
  collect() # fetch into R

faik_3yr <- faik %>%
  filter(year %in% !!income_years) %>% # only years the cohort actually needs
  select(familie_id, year, famaekvivadisp_13) %>% # only the columns we use
  collect() # fetch into R

# 3. Attach each row's own 3 years of income, then average PER COHORT ROW -
# not per pnr, so a repeated pnr with two different baseline years gets two
# separate, correctly-windowed averages instead of one mixed-together number.
# Missing-year rule (Table 8, "Missing values"): 1 missing year -> mean of
# the other 2; 2 missing -> the 1 that exists; 0 available -> no value.
# na.rm = TRUE already does that arithmetic; n_years just records how many
# years it used, so you can see how much averaging happened per row.
income_mean <- cohort_income_years %>%
  left_join(bef_3yr, by = c("pnr", "year")) %>% # this row's household, for this specific year
  left_join(faik_3yr, by = c("familie_id", "year")) %>% # then that household's income, same year
  group_by(row_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_years = sum(!is.na(famaekvivadisp_13)), # how many of the 3 years had a value
    mean_income = mean(famaekvivadisp_13, na.rm = TRUE), # mean disposable income over the years that exist
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(mean_income = if_else(n_years == 0L, NA_real_, mean_income)) # mean() of zero values is NaN, not NA - fix it

# 4. Negative income (Table 8, "Negative values"): possible, mostly for the
# self-employed. SEPLINE offers two options, not one fixed rule: exclude
# these individuals, or run the analysis twice - once counting them as low
# income, once as high income - as a sensitivity check. Decide which fits
# your study; do not silently drop or silently keep them.
income_mean %>%
  summarise(n_negative = sum(mean_income < 0, na.rm = TRUE), total = n())

# 5. Reference population for the cutpoints: same years, no pnr filter. This
# stays LAZY - no collect() here. income_years already spans every year any
# baseline year's 3-year window needs (step 1), so this is not a wider PULL
# than the cohort fetch above - but the population itself is all of Denmark,
# not just your cohort, so the filter/join/mean below are deliberately kept
# inside the database instead of materialised in R. filter(), left_join(),
# year(), floor() and mean() all translate to SQL and run there (verified
# against DuckDB); only the small per-stratum result in step 6 is collected.
# If bef and faik turn out to be on different underlying connections in your
# fastreg setup, this join will error asking for copy = TRUE - collect()
# each side first as a fallback, same as the single-year demo above.
bef_population <- bef %>%
  filter(year %in% !!income_years) %>% # same years, no pnr filter this time
  select(pnr, year, familie_id, koen, foed_dag) # koen + foed_dag for the sex x age strata

faik_population <- faik %>%
  filter(year %in% !!income_years) %>%
  select(familie_id, year, famaekvivadisp_13)

population_with_income <- bef_population %>%
  left_join(faik_population, by = c("familie_id", "year"))

# 6. Each population member's OWN 3-year average - the same rolling window
# as step 3, computed once per distinct baseline year the cohort actually
# uses (baseline_years), not per calendar year. A single-year population
# income would understate how stable most people's income is year to year,
# and would not be comparable to the cohort's own 3-year-averaged value - so
# this repeats step 3's exact logic for the population side instead of
# simplifying it away. The loop is over baseline_years (typically a handful
# of distinct years), not over every person - each pass filters
# population_with_income to that ref_year's 3 years and fixes age AT that
# ref_year (not year-by-year), so nobody's window splits across two
# age_group bands due to a birthday landing mid-window. collect() happens
# LAST in each pass, after the group_by/summarise(mean(...)) has already run
# inside the database - what reaches R per pass is one row per (person,
# stratum), not the raw multi-year population join.
baseline_years <- unique(cohort$year_baseline)

population_income <- lapply(baseline_years, function(by) {
  population_with_income %>%
    filter(year %in% !!c(by, by - 1, by - 2)) %>% # !! evaluates by LOCALLY first - see AKM step 2's index_year for why
    mutate(
      age = by - year(foed_dag), # age AT ref_year, fixed across the whole window
      age_group = floor(age / 5) * 5 # 5-year bands: 0, 5, 10, ...
    ) %>%
    group_by(pnr, koen, age_group) %>%
    summarise(mean_income = mean(famaekvivadisp_13, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    collect() %>% # only the per-person summary leaves the database, not the raw rows
    mutate(ref_year = by)
}) %>%
  bind_rows()

# 7. Cutpoints: Q20/Q40/Q60/Q80 per sex x age group x year, from the
# reference population - these define what "low/medium/high income" means,
# independent of your own cohort's distribution
cutpoints <- population_income %>%
  group_by(koen, age_group, ref_year) %>%
  summarise(
    q20 = quantile(mean_income, 0.2, na.rm = TRUE),
    q40 = quantile(mean_income, 0.4, na.rm = TRUE),
    q60 = quantile(mean_income, 0.6, na.rm = TRUE),
    q80 = quantile(mean_income, 0.8, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# 8. Classify the STUDY cohort against those cutpoints - not against its own
# ntile(), which would only compare people to each other. koen and foed_dag
# come from the same bef_3yr fetch as familie_id (step 2), taken at each
# row's own baseline year.
income_quintile <- cohort %>%
  select(row_id, pnr, year_baseline) %>%
  left_join(
    bef_3yr %>% select(pnr, year, koen, foed_dag),
    by = c("pnr", "year_baseline" = "year")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    age = year_baseline - lubridate::year(foed_dag), # age reached in the baseline year
    age_group = floor(age / 5) * 5 # 5-year bands, matching step 6
  ) %>%
  left_join(income_mean, by = "row_id") %>%
  left_join(cutpoints, by = c("koen", "age_group", "year_baseline" = "ref_year")) %>%
  mutate(
    income_cat = case_when(
      is.na(mean_income) ~ "Unknown", # no income years available at all - see the NA-vs-Unknown callout above
      mean_income <= q20 ~ "Low", # quintile 1
      mean_income > q80 ~ "High", # quintile 5
      TRUE ~ "Medium" # quintiles 2-4 (Table 9's suggested 3-category grouping)
    )
  ) %>%
  select(row_id, mean_income, income_cat)

stopifnot(nrow(income_quintile) == nrow(cohort))
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Two more things SEPLINE flags that this code does not handle for you.**
Inflation: income values should be adjusted to a common year before averaging
across calendar years, using a consumer price index or GDP deflator (Table 8,
Birth Cohort/Life Course Aspects) - not implemented here, since the right
index depends on your study period. Continuous modelling: if you want income
as a continuous variable instead of categories, SEPLINE warns that a linear
term is biased (misclassification is worse at the low end, and the
income-health relationship is not linear) and recommends splines or
fractional polynomials instead.
:::

</details>

## Assemble all SES variables onto the cohort

```r
cohort_ses <- cohort %>%
  left_join(cohort_akm %>% select(row_id, occupation_cat), by = "row_id") %>% # attach employment
  left_join(cohort_udda %>% select(row_id, education_cat), by = "row_id") %>% # attach education
  left_join(income_quintile %>% select(row_id, income_cat), by = "row_id") # attach income quintile

# Sanity check: a correct join never changes the row count
stopifnot(nrow(cohort_ses) == nrow(cohort))
```

Joined on `row_id`, not `pnr` - see [Before you extract anything](#before-you-extract-anything-give-the-cohort-a-stable-row-id) above for why.
